description:
Two AI/backend building a Marswalk decision copilot.

Looking for one frontend/map-UI person (MapLibre/Leaflet); planning and data pipeline are already designed
summary:
BingoTime is a map-based decision companion for astronauts walking on Mars. An EVA plan is made on Earth, but the moment that matters comes in the field: a rock that was not in the plan, a radio link that drops behind a ridge, dust that starts to rise. At that moment BingoTime raises one decision card with a few options — keep the plan, take the fastest or the gentlest route, go to the place a hypothesis points to, stay a little longer, or return to the rover — and shows what each option costs on the same ruler: walking time, margin before the latest safe departure, and science value (a relative index).

The map is built from NASA and USGS data of Jezero crater: a 1 m HiRISE elevation mosaic, the USGS geologic map, an orbital mineral map, and one real day of Perseverance weather. The suit device computes everything offline with a small deterministic C++ core, so it keeps working when the link to the rover is lost. The tool only proposes; the plan changes when the astronaut chooses.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

BingoTime supports one kind of moment in a Mars surface EVA: the moment when the plan and the field stop agreeing. It runs on two computers that share one map — a device on the suit and a computer on the rover — and it speaks only when there is something to decide.

A decision card is raised when

• the crew logs an observation that changes where science value is expected,

• the UHF link to the rover is lost or comes back,

• dust optical depth stays above a threshold,

• the latest safe departure time or sunset is getting close,

• the crew asks for options, or sends their own stop order.

Each card holds a small set of options: continue the plan, fastest route, gentlest route, go to the hypothesis target, stay, drop the last stop, return to the rover, or "my plan" (stops ordered by the crew). Every option is shown with numbers computed the same way: walking time ("about N min M s"), margin before the latest safe departure, distance, and science value (relative index). An option that cannot get the crew back in time is not offered. The plan changes only when the astronaut picks an option.

HOW IT WORKS

(1) Ground pipeline (Python). Before the EVA, source data for a 5 km square area is turned into one read-only bundle: slope, roughness, shadow by time of day, a radio-link map from the rover parking point, geologic units, mineral classes, a sun table, map tiles, and one day of recorded weather. Layers that were drawn on different base images are registered to the elevation mosaic automatically, and the remaining offset is written into the bundle metadata.

(2) Core (C++17, one C header). Route search on a grid with an anytime weighted A*, then the route is pulled straight and its time is measured along the straight line, because a grid path is longer than the real shortest path. Walking speed depends on slope. The core also computes the return time from every cell, the latest safe departure time, the science-value map and its update after each observation, and the choice of options. It allocates no memory after start-up, has bounded loops, and gives the same output for the same input.

(3) Two programs. The suit device uses a 5 m grid and works alone when the link is down. The rover uses a 2 m grid and adds alternatives the device cannot afford to compute. When the link comes back, the rover decides again on fresh telemetry.

(4) Screens (React, TypeScript, Leaflet, three.js). A field screen for the suit and a console screen for the rover or habitat, both drawn on the same map. The console can also show the terrain in 3D with the science-value map laid over it.

(5) Simulator. Scenarios replay an EVA without a person: a walk modelled on Apollo 17 Station 4, a link-loss walk, and two demonstration walks. A separate calculator checks the results.

DATA AND THE PLACE

The area is the western side of Jezero crater, between the Perseverance landing site and the delta. The weather replay is Perseverance sol 313 (January 2022), a day when a regional dust storm reached Jezero: the morning is clear and dust thickens around 11:00 local time. The sun table for that day is computed with the published NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm. The same scenarios also run on two other areas inside the crater (floor and inlet).

WHERE THE NUMBERS COME FROM

• EVA length, walking speed and walking range: NASA xEVA System Concept of Operations (EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B).

• Slope and walking speed, 20° slope limit: NASA ICES-2025-129 and the SEXTANT speed table.

• Warning 20 minutes and last call 7 minutes before the latest departure: Apollo 17 EVA-2 Station 4 (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal).

• Dust threshold: the 95th percentile of the measured dust record at Jezero (Smith 2022); it must hold for one measurement interval before a card is raised.

• Suit–rover UHF link: path-loss model of Foore & Ida 2007 (NASA/TM-2007-214825).

• Every parameter is labelled with where its value comes from: a reference (12 values), a design decision (17) or a tuning value chosen by the team (50). Two thresholds with no reference are left empty — for example, there is no radiation dose warning: dose is displayed only.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

• It is not a safety system. The xEVA concept of operations treats the crew information system as non-safety-critical and separate from the caution and warning system; BingoTime follows that.

• It must work without a link. Everything needed in the field is in the bundle on the device.

• It must not push. Options are filtered by feasibility, not ranked by the tool's preference, and tests check that the order of options carries no bias.

• "Science value" is a relative index built from the geologic unit, the mineral class and the crew's own observations. It is not a calibrated probability, and the starting table has not been reviewed by a geologist.

• Time is shown to the nearest 10 seconds as "about", because a walking-time estimate is not more exact than that.

VERIFICATION

• Core self-test: 3,728 checks pass (also under AddressSanitizer).

• Python tests: 60 pass, 3 skipped — path validity, anytime behaviour, failover when the link is lost, hypothesis handling, no bias in options, scenarios, determinism.

• Four scenarios pass on three areas of Jezero crater (12 runs).

HOW TO TRY IT

• In a browser: open https://26nasa-production.up.railway.app/ and pick a map, a scenario, then a screen (field screen or rover console). "Free run — nothing scripted" starts at the rover with a plan and scripts nothing: you log observations, state hypotheses, replan and choose cards yourself.

• The public server runs one simulation shared by everyone who has it open, and it sleeps when idle, so the first visit can take a moment.

• On your own machine: clone https://github.com/Namung2/26NASA and follow README.md (build the core, build the screens, start the live server). The three map bundles come with the repository and are unpacked on first run.

TOOLS

C++17, CMake, Python 3.12 (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio/GDAL, pyogrio, scikit-image, Pillow, pydantic, FastAPI, uvicorn), TypeScript, React, Leaflet, three.js, Vite.

USE OF AI

Most of the code, tests and English text in the repository were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Anthropic) under the team's direction and review. The assistant was also used to find and read references. The product itself contains no AI or machine-learning model: every number on the screen comes from deterministic computation on the data listed below. No AI-generated image, video or audio is included.
